sections.title: Which one do I need?
sections.content: You know passive and impersonal *se* from B2 Unit 19: the verb agrees with a thing and stays singular with no noun or with personal *a*. Now you have three ways to speak about people without naming them, and each one says something different. *Se* is neutral: it is nobody in particular, and fits rules and general facts. A plural verb points to other people, never to you. *Uno* includes you. Choosing well means asking one question: who do I want to be part of this?

sections.title: Same idea, three choices
rows: People live well here. (a general statement)
The people here live well. (other people)
You live well here, and I do too. (including me)

sections.title: Se, ser and estar
sections.content: Impersonal *se* also works with *ser* and *estar* plus an adjective. The adjective stays in the masculine singular: *Cuando se es joven, se aprende rápido*. *Cuando se está cansado, se trabaja peor*. This is new in this lesson. With *uno* you can say the same thing: *Cuando uno está cansado, trabaja peor*.

items.spanish: Cuando se es joven, se aprende rápido.
items.english: When you are young, you learn quickly.

items.spanish: Cuando se está lejos, se extraña a la familia.
items.english: When you are far away, you miss your family.

items.spanish: Cuando uno se muda a otra ciudad, extraña a su familia.
items.english: When you move to another city, you miss your family.

items.spanish: Me robaron el celular en el autobús.
items.english: Somebody stole my phone on the bus.

sections.content: Use the plural, not *se*, when someone did something to you: *Me robaron el celular*. And use *se* for rules, as in the notices of B2 Unit 19, because they apply to everybody. If you want to say that you feel something yourself, *uno* sounds more personal: *Uno se cansa*.
